item.content:encoded:
Last night was a good night for the Yankees, seeing the team put up five runs in the first paired with a good Gerrit Cole outing to cruise to a 9-2 win over the Diamondbacks. The club also picked up a game on the Rays as the AL East leaders dropped the opener of their series to the Red Sox. Tonight, the Yankees have two goals: get the win to stay in a hypothetically-competitive division race (all but necessary since Tampa Bay avenged the loss with a 2-1 win over Boston this afternoon), and build out a little more breathing room in the Cy Young race.
Dylan Cease had his worst start of the year on Friday for the Blue Jays, going just 2.2 innings and walking six. He and today's Yankee starter Cam Schlittler have had a heavyweight bout atop the Cy leaderboard all year, and while Cam's pulled away a bit in recent weeks, he can start to put the finishing touches on his case tonight. He hasn't allowed more than one earned run in a start since August 3rd (!!), making us all maybe expect a bit too much from the righty who can seemingly do no wrong. Schlittler has thrown 45 innings across those aforementioned seven starts, so he's not a five-and-fly guy, and his 1.00 ERA in that stretch is just…a farce.
Brandon Pfaadt is having the best season of his young career, with a 3.77 ERA and 4.06 FIP that are both significant steps forward after a pretty lost 2025. He doesn't strike many men out though, and a 45 percent ground ball rate means heavy sinking fastballs in the zone. There will be pitches to hit from Pfaadt; you just need to be able to elevate them.
Ben Rice had himself a fantastic game cleaning up last night and is bumped up to the leadoff spot tonight, with
Luis García Jr. getting the nod over Paul Goldschmidt at first base. Spencer Jones reportedly has a sore left foot, which means we get José Caballero in center, and I'm going to withhold comment on that decision for now.
It's an 8:10pm Eastern start but not a national broadcast, this one's on YES. The Diamondbacks will be celebrating their 2001 World Series championship throughout the evening, which seems kind of lame because you can't really "win" a championship when you didn't have an opponent.

item.title: [The Big Lead] Yankees make sudden change to lineup, remove breakout star
item.dc:creator: Lou Landers
item.description: The Yankees are already dealing with the loss of Aaron Judge, and now they have another outfielder on the MLB roster who is temporarily unavailable. Spencer Jones, one of New York’s biggest breakout stories over the past month, is out of Saturday’s lineup against the Arizona Diamondbacks with left foot soreness. The rookie told MLB.com’s Bryan Hoch that he expects it to be a one-day issue, which should provide some relief for a Yankees team that cannot afford another significant injury. Spencer
item.content:encoded:
The Yankees are already dealing with the loss of Aaron Judge, and now they have another outfielder on the MLB roster who is temporarily unavailable. Spencer Jones, one of New York’s biggest breakout stories over the past month, is out of Saturday’s lineup against the Arizona Diamondbacks with left foot soreness.
The rookie told MLB.com’s Bryan Hoch that he expects it to be a one-day issue, which should provide some relief for a Yankees team that cannot afford another significant injury.
Spencer Jones has become a key part of Yankees’ lineup
Jones’ emergence has been one of the more encouraging developments for New York this season. After struggling early in his rookie campaign, the 25-year-old has started to find his footing at the plate and has become the Yankees’ everyday center fielder.
Through his first 80 games, Jones is hitting .248/.318/.433 with 10 home runs and a 109 wRC+. More importantly, his September has been particularly impressive. He entered Saturday batting .340/.415/.532 with two homers, 12 RBIs and seven runs through his first 13 games of the month.
The Yankees have also been encouraged by the adjustments Jones has made against Major League pitching. Manager Aaron Boone previously compared his developmental path to Judge’s, noting that Jones’ enormous 6-foot-7 frame could become a major advantage as his adjustments continue to translate.
That makes Saturday’s lineup change particularly notable.
Yankees cannot afford another outfield injury
Jones is being held out as a precaution, with José Caballero taking over in center field Saturday. Jones has indicated that he expects to return Sunday, so there is currently no indication that the foot issue is expected to become a lengthy absence.
Still, the timing is less than ideal.
Judge officially returned to the injured list Saturday with a right calf strain and has no established timetable for his return. The Yankees recalled Max Schuemann to fill his roster spot, while the club is expected to rely more heavily on its remaining outfield options.
New York has already dealt with significant injuries across its roster this season. With the postseason approaching, the Yankees need Jones healthy and available because his recent production has given the lineup another legitimate offensive option.
For now, the hope is that Jones’ absence truly is nothing more than a one-day precaution.

That was a
item.content:encoded:
PHOENIX — Without any guarantees of it happening, Aaron Judge is holding out hope of returning from a calf strain in time for the playoffs.
“I’d like to be back by the postseason; that’s definitely the plan,” Judge said Saturday afternoon. “We’re going to do everything we can to get back as soon as we can.”
Access the Yankees beat like never before
Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees.
That was a slightly less definitive statement than what Judge consistently said during the summer when he was trying to come back from a right rib stress fracture, which he did after three-plus months on Sept. 8.
But now the clock is ticking even louder, with Saturday marking 10 days away from Game 1 of the American League wild card series.
“Definitely frustrated,” said Judge, who played seven games after missing 84 on the IL with the rib injury. “Dealt with strains before and kind of played through them, but this was in a different spot where it made it a little bit more difficult.”
Judge did not reveal what grade the strain was, but said it involved his Soleus muscle, which he indicated was more important to running and hitting compared to the gastrocnemius muscle.
“The focus is still the same, to be ready to go for October,” Judge said.
In the meantime, the Yankees are banking on their summer without Judge paying off now that he is back on the IL.
“Lean on each other,” Cody Bellinger said. “The game itself is hard; if you add too much pressure on yourself, the game becomes even harder. So we really just have to play for each other, lean on each other, pass the baton, do your job and control what you can control.”
The Yankees did that on Friday night, racing out of the gates to score five runs in the first inning of a 9-2 win against the Diamondbacks, just hours after the team announced Judge was going on the 10-day injured list with a right calf strain.
But they also got off well at the beginning of June after Judge landed on the IL with a right rib stress fracture before their lineup became a black hole for an extended stretch during the summer. They had finally started to break out of it shortly before Judge got back on Sept. 8, but after having him back for seven games, they now find themselves in the same spot again, less than two weeks away from the start of the playoffs.
“We’ve played most of the year this way, and I feel like in a lot of cases, especially some of our key guys over the last few weeks have started to, especially offensively, get it going like we know they’re capable of,” manager Aaron Boone said.
During the 84-game span that Judge missed this summer, the Yankees ranked 26th in runs per game (4.06), 29th in batting average (.227), 27th in OPS (.681), and 29th in WRC+ (90).
But over the tail end of that stretch, and into Judge’s return, the Yankees started to hit more like they are capable of. That included the trade deadline addition of Luis García Jr., the emergence of rookie outfielder Spencer Jones, and Bellinger getting back on track after returning from his own hamstring injury in August.
Perhaps most importantly, it has coincided with the reemergence of Ben Rice. The lefty slugger was a game wrecker for the first two months of the season before Judge went down, then cooled off a bit during the summer (albeit with some good stretches along the way) before catching fire again over the last few weeks. Entering Saturday, over his last 22 games, Rice had hit .353 with a 1.037 OPS and five home runs, including his 39th of the season Friday night.
“Special year,” Gerrit Cole said. “Has made some really good adjustments from previous years, going into this year, and I think he’s really started to heat back up here the last few weeks after having to make some adjustments in the middle of the season. Not only is he really proficient with the bat, but he’s a smart player and a hard worker, which is leading him to have a really outstanding season for us.”
The Yankees need that to continue for however long Judge is out (and even if and when he returns) for them to play deep into October, though Rice isn’t looking at it as having to do any more — which got some hitters in trouble during the three-time AL MVP’s first absence.
“I would think that everyone just goes out there and stays within themselves, tries to put together quality at-bat after quality at-bat,” he said. “Pitching is always going to be doing their thing, like they have for us all year. So from an offensive standpoint, just do what we did [Friday]: go out and have a team at-bat, trust the guy behind you and keep the line moving.”
To Rice’s point, the Yankees have leaned on the strength of their pitching staff all season, but that was especially the case during Judge’s three months on the IL this summer, when they were able to scratch out enough wins in low-scoring games, with their pitchers keeping them in it almost every night.
New York Post may be compensated and/or receive an affiliate commission if you buy something through our links.
“We have a lot of confidence in here,” Cole said. “For the most part of the summer, we’ve been tested really, really hard and we responded, by and large, really, really well. We have a lot of perfectionists in here. We’re always striving to be perfect and trying to be the best. But the reality is we’ve had a lot of obstacles we’ve had to overcome and, by and large, we’ve played really well.”

item.title: [Yanks Go Yard] Spencer Jones' remarkable stats vs. lefties are better than Yankees fans' wildest dreams
item.dc:creator: Stephen Parello
item.description: There were many questions the New York Yankees needed Spencer Jones to answer this season. Now, we've seen enough of him, even if it's been in a couple of disjointed stints, to get a good idea of who he is at the major league level. The answer: pretty damn good. After struggling early, Jones has found his footing. A big reason for his ascendancy has been surprising. The Vanderbilt product has mashed left-handed pitching. He's now logged 51 plate appearances against lefties and has slashed an eye
item.content:encoded:
There were many questions the New York Yankees needed Spencer Jones to answer this season. Now, we've seen enough of him, even if it's been in a couple of disjointed stints, to get a good idea of who he is at the major league level.
The answer: pretty damn good. After struggling early, Jones has found his footing. A big reason for his ascendancy has been surprising. The Vanderbilt product has mashed left-handed pitching.
He's now logged 51 plate appearances against lefties and has slashed an eye-watering .435/.490/.761 following his homer off Minnesota Twins lefty specialist Taylor Rodgers on Sept. 15. It was the first dinger Rodgers gave up to a left-handed hitter over 133 plate appearances this season.
The sample size isn't huge, but it's relatively significant. For example, Ben Rice has 209 plate appearances against lefties out of his 622 plate appearances. For Jones, the 51 matchups against southpaws are a decent portion of his 255 total plate appearances.
One of the most impressive things about how he's performed against same-handed pitching is the amount of power he's demonstrated. Obviously, the six-foot-seven outfielder is a behemoth, but most lefties, even those who perform well against southpaws, see a drop in power in those situations. Take Rice, for instance; his slugging percentage drops from .561 against righties to .457 against left-handers. That hasn't been the case for Jones.
This has just been one part of Jones' maturation process that should have every fan feeling confident about not only his future, but his ability to contribute now.
Spencer Jones' performance against lefties has Yankees well-positioned for playoffs vs. Red Sox
Overall, Jones is hitting .259/.331/.452 with 10 homers on the season. He's been even better since being recalled on July 22, posting a .271/.337/.490 line with eight of his 10 homers coming during this most recent span.
There should be no more doubt that he should start over Trent Grisham, assuming Grisham is healthy, once the playoffs roll around. A significant part of that reasoning has to do with his performance against southpaws.
Jones has learned a lot from Cody Bellinger on how to handle those tough at-bats since he's been up in the bigs and the star left fielder has been healthy.
“When we are in the dugout, he’s one of those people I can go up to and ask, like, ‘Yo, what did you see?’ He’ll tell me bluntly what he saw, how he saw it, and essentially what he’s going to do next time. It’s like, all right, good to know before I go even into my first (at-bat) what this MVP is going to do for his first at-bat. It’s pretty sweet knowing that I’ve got these guys to help me out,” Jones said to The Athletic this week.
He couldn't have a better mentor. Bellinger isn't hitting lefties as much as he did last year, when he put up an insane .353/.415/.601 line, but his .287/.346/.449 performance in 2026 is plenty good, and better than what he's done against righties. In fact, Bellinger is about as balanced as they come with an .804 career OPS against left-handers and an .819 mark against righties.
We spoke about Rice earlier, but the early-season drama about his usage against lefties is a thing of the past. While he has more pop against righties, Rice's .255/.330/.457 line against southpaws is more than serviceable.
Despite having so many lefties in the lineup on a daily basis, the Yankees as a whole don't suffer much from it. The club is hitting a collective .247/.318/.422 against left-handed pitching this season, with a .740 OPS that ranks ninth. Remember, for most of that time, Aaron Judge hasn't been a factor, either.
Looking ahead, the Yankees' most likely opponent in the Wild Card series is the Red Sox, who are loaded with left-handers. In the rotation, they boast southpaws Payton Tolle and Ranger Suárez, with their being a possibility that Jake Bennett makes the cut, too. In the bullpen, they'll hope to unleash Garrett Crochet, Erik Miller and old friend Aroldis Chapman.
However, rather than being overmatched, we might say that this plays into the Yankees' hands. New York can handle left-handed pitching, and those lefty bats can tee off against righties. Jones emerging as a threat against southpaws only solidifies the strength and gives the Yankees another regular who doesn't need a platoon partner, allowing them to match up only where they're vulnerable.

item.dc:creator: Jackson Kruse

New York Yankees Announce Interesting José Caballero Decision Surprisingly, José Caballero will start in center field for the Yankees on Saturday. Caballero has pla
item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees are in the middle of a three-game series against the Arizona Diamondbacks at Chase Field in Phoenix.
New York won the first game of the series 9-2 on Friday. Game 2 is slated to begin at 8:10 p.m. EDT on Saturday.
Before Saturday’s game, the Yankees announced a surprising lineup decision involving José Caballero.
New York Yankees Announce Interesting José Caballero Decision
Surprisingly, José Caballero will start in center field for the Yankees on Saturday. Caballero has played 11 innings in center this season and recorded 15 innings at the position last year.
Meanwhile, Spencer Jones, the Yankees’ primary center fielder, is out of the lineup with a sore left foot.
The New York Post’s Greg Joyce wrote on X: Spencer Jones said he’s dealing with a sore left foot, which he chalked up to the wear-and-tear from playing on turf. But downplayed it, said he’s fine, just getting a day. “It’s no big deal,” Jones said.
Here is the Yankees’ full lineup for Saturday:
- Ben Rice DH
- Cody Bellinger LF
- Luis Garcia Jr. 1B
- Heliot Ramos RF
- George Lombard Jr. SS
- Austin Wells C
- Anthony Volpe 2B
- Ryan McMahon 3B
- José Caballero CF
Starting Pitcher: RHP Cam Schlittler
Here is the Diamondbacks’ lineup:
- Laars Nootbar LF
- Ketel Marte 2B
- Gabriel Moreon C
- Geraldo Perdomo SS
- Corbin Carroll RF
- Nolan Arenado 3B
- Tim Tawa 1B
- Jesus Sanchez DH
- Jordan Lawlar CF
Starting Pitcher: Brandon Pfaadt
New York Yankees Right Now
In the division standings, New York is four games back of the Tampa Bay Rays for first place in the AL East.
Next, the Yankees are slated to play the Diamondbacks at 8:10 p.m. EDT on Saturday. The series will wrap up on Sunday afternoon.
The Yankees will finish the season by hosting the Tampa Bay Rays for four games, and then the Baltimore Orioles for three games.
If the standings hold up, the Yankees will host the Red Sox in the Wild Card round.

item.title: [CBS Sports] Three questions for Aaron Judge and the Yankees as injury casts doubt on slugger's playoff availability
item.dc:creator: Mike Axisa
item.description: Friday was a bad day for the New York Yankees even though they opened their final road series of the regular season with a blowout win (NYY 9, ARI 2). item.content:encoded:
Friday was a bad day for the New York Yankees even though they opened their final road series of the regular season with a blowout win (NYY 9, ARI 2). Captain Aaron Judge is less than two weeks after returning from a fractured rib that sidelined him more than three months. Judge's status for the rest of the season is up in the air.
"I don't have a timeline on him. I'm not going to predict anything. We'll just obviously treat it and see what transpires," manager Aaron Boone said (via MLB.com). "... The reality is, we've had to play a lot of the season this year without him. There's no replacing a player who is as great as Aaron Judge, but we have high expectations. Those don't change now."
The Yankees are always cagey about Judge's injuries. They declined to reveal the severity of the calf strain or give a timetable for his return. Generally speaking, Grade 1 calf strains (the least severe) require 2-3 weeks on the injured list, though calves are very tricky and easy to reinjury. They must be allowed to heal fully, otherwise you risk a more severe injury.
For all intents and purposes, the Yankees are locked into the top wild-card spot. They're six games up in the loss column on the Boston Red Sox, who currently sit in the second wild card spot, plus the Yankees won the season series and have the tiebreaker, so it's really a seven-game lead. New York can clinch the top wild-card spot as soon as Sunday.
The AL East title remains mathematically possible, but it is a long shot. The Yankees are four games behind the Tampa Bay Rays in the loss column with four head-to-head games remaining next week in the Bronx. The Rays only need to win one of those four games to clinch the season series and secure the tiebreaker, upping the difficulty for New York.
Just to lay it all out, here's what needs to happen for the Yankees to win the AL East, assuming they sweep those four games against the Rays and clinch the tiebreaker for themselves, which is a pretty big assumption:
- Rays go 6-3 or better: Rays win AL East
- Rays go 5-4: Yankees must go 9-0
- Rays go 4-5: Yankees must go 8-1
- Rays go 3-6: Yankees must go 7-2
- Rays go 2-7: Yankees must go 6-3
- Rays go 1-8: Yankees must go 5-4
- Rays go 0-9: Yankees must go 4-5
The Yankees have already clinched a postseason spot and winning the AL East was a long shot even with Judge. These last nine regular-season games are almost meaningless. If the AL East race gets interesting in a few days, the Yankees can shift gears, but the big picture takes priority this next week. Resting key relievers, lining up the rotation for the Wild Card Series, etc.
"Missing Judge, it hurts. We all know he's the best hitter in the game," Cody Bellinger said (via MLB.com). "For us in here, our mindset is, we're going to have to find a way. I think the talent in this locker room speaks for itself. I'm fully confident that we have enough talent in here that we can go out and win, and beat anybody."
With the postseason less than two weeks away, Judge's calf injury creates a lot of questions for both him and the Yankees overall. Here are three questions for the man himself, and his team.
Three questions for Judge
1. Will he return for the postseason? This is really the only question, right? The Yankees are built around Judge being the best hitter in the world, and when he's not, the walls begin to cave in. New York had one of the lowest-scoring offenses in baseball when Judge was out with his rib injury. To paraphrase another New York baseball legend, Judge is the straw that stirs the drink.
Judge is eligible to come off the injured list next Sunday, the final day of the regular season. Roster-wise, he can return in time for the postseason. Health-wise, we have no idea. Calf strains are rarely 10-day absences, but that's what the Yankees have to hope is the case here. There's a very real chance the Yankees are without Judge for at least the Wild Card Series, and maybe longer.
“I’d like to be back by the postseason,” Aaron Judge said. “That’s definitely the plan.”
Said the calf strain involves the soleus muscle — which he said is more crucial to running and hitting — making it more difficult to play through.
2. Will he be himself at the plate? Judge did not go on a minor-league rehab assignment before returning from the rib injury and it showed. He went 4 for 23 (.174) with one walk and 13 strikeouts in his seven games back before the calf injury. His timing was not there at all. Judge's one homer came on a hanging breaking ball. Otherwise, pitchers threw fastballs by him consistently.
To put a number on it, Judge missed with 41% of his swings against fastballs in his seven games back, more than double the 19% league average. This is what it looks like when you miss with more than two out of every five swings against heaters:
It is not exactly a surprise a hitter who did not go on a rehab assignment after spending more than three months on the shelf looked out of sorts at the plate. Judge and the Yankees knew it would take him some time to get back up to speed at the plate, and they were willing to live with it. The goal was always to be ready for the postseason, not so much the regular season.
These last nine games aren't particularly important for the Yankees in the standings, but they were incredibly important to Judge. He needed at-bats to rediscover his timing at the plate, and get back to being the dominant hitter he's been throughout his career. The calf strain puts that on pause. Judge now has even fewer at-bats available to get back to being himself.
3. Will he be able to play the field? There is a scenario in which Judge plays through the calf strain as a full-time DH who doesn't run at 100% (or close to it). How the Yankees would align their defense in that scenario, I have no idea. Ben Rice is a full-time DH these days and also New York's best non-Judge hitter. Platoon-mates Luis Gárcia Jr. and Paul Goldschmidt are first basemen.
Unless the Yankees do something unexpected, like put Gárcia back at second base (where he was terrible defensively) or Rice back behind the plate (where he was also terrible defensively), slotting Judge in at DH means one of the team's most productive hitters will have to sit. This is something the Yankees will worry about when the time comes, and not a second sooner.
Three questions for the Yankees
1. Where will the righty pop come from? The Yankees have a very lefty-heavy lineup and Judge's righty heft provides important balance. Only the Cleveland Guardians have gotten fewer plate appearances from righties this season. Friday's lineup against Arizona Diamondbacks lefty Eduardo Rodriguez could be what the Yankees run out there against lefties in October:
- 1B Paul Goldschmidt, RHB
- LF Cody Bellinger, LHB
- RF Heliot Ramos, RHB
- DH Ben Rice, LHB
- 3B Amed Rosario, RHB
- CF Spencer Jones, LHB
- SS George Lombard Jr., RHB
- C Austin Wells, LHB
- 2B Anthony Volpe, RHB
Goldschmidt and Ramos are lefty mashers. Bellinger and Rice are very productive left-on-left hitters. Jones has performed well against lefties as a big leaguer, though his minor-league track record against southpaws isn't great. Rosario is having his worst season against lefties. The 7-8-9 spots are unlikely to make an impact offensively, regardless of the pitcher's handedness.
That lineup would look much more imposing with Judge in the No. 3 spot. Perhaps this is not such a big concern though? Since trade deadline day, the Yankees have the highest batting average (.289) and on-base percentage (.362) against lefties, and the third-highest slugging percentage (.456) despite Judge not playing much, and not being much of a factor when he did play.
In all likelihood the Yankees will host the Red Sox in the Wild Card Series, and Boston has three quality lefty starters (Jake Bennett, Ranger Suárez, Payton Tolle) and a shutdown lefty relief tandem (Aroldis Chapman, Erik Miller). To beat the Red Sox, the Yankees will need their righty hitters to produce, and now the status of their best right-handed hitter is in question.
2. Will the pitching hold up? Despite not having Judge for more than three months, the Yankees have the American League's best run differential (+143) and second-best record (89-64). They can thank their pitching staff. New York has allowed only 3.68 runs per game this year, the fewest in baseball. Since trade deadline day, it's an incredible 3.37 runs allowed per game.
There are some cracks beginning to form, however. Gerrit Cole has surrendered eight home runs in his last three starts, including five on a four-seam fastball that is no longer the dominant pitch it was at his peak. Max Fried's velocity has been down a tick since returning from a bone bruise in his elbow late last month. That injury has sent him to the injured list twice this year.
Cam Schlittler, the AL Cy Young favorite, has thrown a career-high 184 ⅔ innings with two regular-season starts remaining, plus the postseason. Key late-inning relievers Paul Blackburn, David Bednar, and Brent Headrick have worked a lot -- A LOT -- this season and have all shown a slight dip in velocity in recent weeks, which perhaps is a sign the workload is catching up to them.
Without Judge (and sometimes even with him), the Yankees are a run prevention team. Their superpower is a suffocating pitching staff that is among the best in baseball at limiting hard contact, particularly in the air. With Judge absent, the pitching staff and the ability to prevent runs in general will be of paramount importance. No Judge reduces the margin of error considerably.
3. What about their other injured players? Judge is not the only injured Yankee. Center field Trent Grisham has not played since Sept. 4 due to a Grade 2 hamstring strain. On Friday, Boone said Grisham is pretty far into his running program, and he could make it back before the end of the regular season. That would give the outfield a lift should Judge miss extended time.
Second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. has not played since jamming his thumb sliding into second base on Sept. 8. Boone said Chisholm will come off the injured list when the Yankees return home next week. He's had a down year overall, but Chisholm was playing his best baseball of the season right before the injury. He's an important presence given his speed and defense in particular.
Left-hander Ryan Weathers is working his way back from a flexor strain. He last pitched Aug. 22. Weathers is throwing bullpen sessions, though Boone confirmed he won't return during the regular season. If/when Weathers does return, it will be as a reliever. He has bullpen experience and the Yankees could use middle relief help, but Weathers has to make it back first.
At minimum, Chisholm and Grisham would give the Yankees more options for their Judge-less lineup, even if they only platoon. It wouldn't be hard to find a role for Weathers, who had allowed no more than one run in six of his last seven starts before the injury. Bottom line though, the Yankees need Judge. Everything else is secondary to his return and effectiveness.

item.title: [Pinstripes Nation] Últimas Noticias Sobre Las Lesiones De Los Yankees: Dos Jugadores Se Perderán El Resto De La Temporada Y Otros Dos Están A Punto De Volver
item.dc:creator: Esteban Quiñones
item.description: PHOENIX — La lista de lesionados en el vestuario de los Yankees cuenta dos historias a la vez. Por un lado, se está vaciando. Por el otro, acaba de llenarse más. item.content:encoded:
PHOENIX — La lista de lesionados en el vestuario de los Yankees cuenta dos historias a la vez. Por un lado, se está vaciando. Por el otro, acaba de llenarse más. El mismo fin de semana en que dos titulares se acercaban a su regreso, el equipo se enteró de que terminaría la temporada regular sin su capitán.
Para unos Yankees que persiguen el título de división y se preparan para octubre, este momento tiene sus pros y sus contras. Llegan refuerzos tanto para el cuadro como para los jardines. Pero no volverán una pieza clave de la defensa ni un pilar de la rotación de lanzadores.
Chisholm y Grisham, a punto de volver
La buena noticia viene del lado de los jugadores de campo. Jazz Chisholm Jr., de baja desde el 10 de septiembre por un esguince en el pulgar derecho, volverá al equipo durante la serie en casa que empieza el martes contra los Rays. Boone dijo que Chisholm había bateado cuatro días seguidos y que ya había vuelto a lanzar.
Chisholm estaba en racha cuando se lesionó: había promediado un promedio de bateo de 0,375, con un porcentaje de embasado de 0,464 y un jonrón en sus últimos siete partidos. Su regreso devuelve a los Yankees a su segunda base titular justo en el momento más importante de la temporada.
«Veremos cuáles son nuestras necesidades y cómo se le ve, y si creemos que está listo para incorporarse y aportar su granito de arena», dijo Boone.
Grisham le sigue de cerca. El jardinero central lleva fuera desde el 5 de septiembre por una distensión de grado 2 en el isquiotibial derecho, y Boone ha dicho que ya está muy avanzado en su programa de recuperación con carreras. Ahora los Yankees barajan la posibilidad de que vuelva antes de que termine la temporada regular.
Judge, de baja por una distensión en la pantorrilla
La noticia más impactante es la de Aaron Judge. El tres veces MVP de la Liga Americana entra en la lista de lesionados de 10 días por una distensión en la pantorrilla derecha, una decisión que los Yankees hicieron oficial el sábado, aunque con efecto retroactivo desde el jueves. Así que su regreso más temprano podría ser en el último partido de la temporada regular, el 27 de septiembre.
Judge tuvo que abandonar el partido del miércoles, que acabaron perdiendo en la 13.ª entrada en Minnesota, por una contractura en la parte inferior de la pierna derecha, que, según él, empezó ya en la primera entrada. Una resonancia magnética realizada el jueves en Phoenix confirmó la distensión. Boone no quiso dar detalles sobre la gravedad ni sobre el tiempo de recuperación, y tampoco se comprometió a que volviera para la postemporada.
Cuando le preguntaron directamente si Judge volvería para los playoffs, Boone fue breve.
«No lo sé», dijo Boone. «No tengo un plazo para él. Ahora mismo está en la lista de lesionados. No voy a hacer predicciones. Está recibiendo tratamiento y ya veremos qué pasa».
Su ausencia se nota menos de lo que se habría notado antes. Los Yankees tienen un balance de 48-39 en los partidos que Judge se ha perdido esta temporada y de 41-25 cuando juega. Aun así, Boone se lo puso claro sobre la derrota.
«No hay quien pueda sustituir a un jugador tan bueno como Aaron Judge, pero tenemos grandes expectativas», dijo Boone. «Y eso no va a cambiar ahora».
A Weathers se le acaba la pista
El contratiempo más discreto es el de Ryan Weathers. El zurdo lleva en la lista de lesionados desde el 23 de agosto por una distensión en los flexores del antebrazo izquierdo, y Boone admitió el viernes que es poco probable que lance en un partido antes de que termine la temporada.
Esto descarta que el lanzador, que sin hacer mucho ruido se había convertido en uno de los brazos más fiables de los Yankees, vuelva a jugar esta temporada regular. Weathers terminó con un balance de 5-8 y una efectividad de 3,60 en 25 salidas como titular —su mejor marca personal—, y registró una efectividad de 2,27 en sus últimas siete salidas antes de la lesión.
No está totalmente descartado para lo que queda de temporada. Weathers tenía previsto hacer una segunda sesión de bullpen el sábado, y el siguiente paso sería una sesión de bateo en vivo. Todavía es posible que tenga un papel en el bullpen durante la postemporada si su preparación avanza más rápido, aunque los Yankees esperarán para valorar su progreso.
La estadística que cambia el panorama del jardín
El regreso de Trent Grisham parecía complicado antes de que Judge se lesionara, porque el novato Spencer Jones aprovechó la oportunidad. Jones ha bateado .361, con un porcentaje de embasado de .425 y un porcentaje de slugging de .528 en los 10 partidos que lleva jugando en el centro del campo.
La ausencia de Judge cambia las cuentas. Ahora hay sitio para los dos. Grisham podría volver a jugar de centro frente a los lanzadores diestros, lo que dejaría a Jones en el campo derecho, donde de otro modo estaría Judge. Una lesión ha creado discretamente un hueco en la alineación que no existía hace una semana.
El jugador de campo interior y exterior Max Schuemann se ha desplazado a Phoenix para unirse a los Yankees de cara al partido del sábado, aportando profundidad al equipo mientras se va definiendo la alineación.
El martes empieza en el Yankee Stadium una serie de cuatro partidos contra los Rays, que incluye una doble jornada, y que podría decidir el título de la división. Los Yankees la afrontarán sin Judge ni Weathers, pero probablemente con Chisholm y quizá Grisham de vuelta en el equipo.
Por ahora, el panorama es mitad optimista, mitad sombrío. Dos jugadores vuelven a cruzar la puerta del vestuario. Otros dos están pendientes del calendario, con la esperanza de que aún haya tiempo para marcar la diferencia en octubre.
¿Qué te parece? Deja tu comentario abajo.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Yankees Are Creating Their Own Distraction With Aaron Judge Injury Secrecy
item.dc:creator: Joseph Randazzo; Unknown
item.description: The New York Yankees haven't exactly been forthright about what's been going on with Aaron Judge. They didn't offer much information when he was initially pulled during the game against the Minnesota Twins. All the public knew was that Judge had tightness in his lower leg, and that was about it. They didn't alleviate any concerns about Judge after he was placed on the injured list. In fact, things have been just as hush. According to the Daily News' Gary Phillips, Judge wasn't available to speak
item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees haven't exactly been forthright about what's been going on with Aaron Judge. They didn't offer much information when he was initially pulled during the game against the Minnesota Twins. All the public knew was that Judge had tightness in his lower leg, and that was about it.
They didn't alleviate any concerns about Judge after he was placed on the injured list. In fact, things have been just as hush.
According to the Daily News' Gary Phillips, Judge wasn't available to speak to the media before the game. He wasn't there for them after their 9-2 win against the Arizona Diamondbacks either. The extent of the calf strain is still unclear.
Aaron Boone didn't offer up much of an answer when asked about Judge. His response was muted and didn't offer insight into whether he'll return in the postseason.
"I don't have a timeline on him," Boone said, according to MLB.com's Bryan Hoch. "I'm not going to predict anything. We'll just obviously treat it and see what transpires."
While the public knowing what's wrong with Judge doesn't change his schedule or the organization's plans heading into the postseason, their secrecy won't keep the team from answering a barrage of questions. In fact, they'll likely get more.
This isn't the type of story that goes away with time, and even though the Yankees beat a tough opponent in Eduardo Rodriguez, that will be the story on all the back pages. There won't be an image of a sullen Rodriguez walking off the mound, but rather an image of Judge plastered on every newspaper. This storm cloud is still following the team.
Ghosting the media is a weird look, too
Plus, Judge avoiding the media looks odd when Jazz Chisholm Jr. or Clint Frazier did the same and took hits for it. When Frazier did it in 2019, a headline in The Athletic said that he "ghosted" reporters. There won't be any of that with Judge.
Not speaking to the media was held against those guys and used to say something about their character. For Judge, their captain, the same standard should apply. If he is going to be the example of how a New York Yankee should carry themselves, he should be front and center for reporters, as anyone else would be.
Obviously, Judge could talk, and the Yankees can offer a realistic timetable for what they think is happening, but that doesn't change his timeline. They'll still have to be without him, and guys like Spencer Jones will need to step up.
Still, come the postseason, it's probably better to mitigate any potential circus around the team. Playing in October is hard enough, and the team already gets enough attention during this time of year. No need to make things harder for themselves.
Joe Randazzo is a reference librarian who lives on Long Island. When he’s not behind a desk offering assistance to his patrons, he writes about the Yankees for Yankees On SI. Follow him as @YankeeLibrarian on X and Instagram.

item.title: [Pinstripes Nation] Gerrit Cole, De Los Yankees, Hace Historia En La MLB, Pero Sigue Teniendo Un Punto Débil Bastante Peligroso
item.dc:creator: Sara Molnick
item.description: PHOENIX — Gerrit Cole llegó al Chase Field con mucho más en juego en su salida del viernes por la noche que el resultado final de un partido de septiembre. item.content:encoded:
PHOENIX — Gerrit Cole llegó al Chase Field con mucho más en juego en su salida del viernes por la noche que el resultado final de un partido de septiembre. Los Yankees ya se habían asegurado una plaza en la postemporada, pero el orden de su rotación aún se estaba definiendo y a Cole solo le quedaba un pequeño margen para afianzar su puesto en ella.
Los Yankees le dieron margen de maniobra desde el principio. Cole supo aprovechar bien esa ventaja para que los Yankees se llevaran una cómoda victoria por 9-2. Lanzó seis entradas, cedió cuatro hits y dos carreras, ponchó a seis y no concedió ninguna base por bolas. El as de los Yankees lanzó 62 de 90 lanzamientos como strikes y eliminó a 13 de los últimos 15 bateadores a los que se enfrentó.
Los Yankees siguieron sumando carreras y Spencer Jones echó una mano a Cole con una atrapada en deslizamiento en la tercera entrada.
Con esta victoria, los Yankees se sitúan con un balance de 89-64, a cuatro partidos de Tampa Bay en la División Este de la Liga Americana y 5 1/2 partidos por delante de Boston en la lucha por la primera plaza de comodín de la Liga Americana. Dado que la serie de comodines está programada para empezar el 29 de septiembre, la última salida de Cole en la temporada regular ya no se centra tanto en acumular minutos de juego como en demostrar que la versión en la que los Yankees pueden confiar en octubre es la que está ahora en el montículo.
Los Yankees ya tienen asegurada su plaza en la postemporada, pero el equipo aún tiene que organizar una rotación sólida para una serie corta, en la que una sola salida floja puede dar al traste con toda la ronda. Cole llegó a Arizona con solo una salida más, después de esta, que pudiera influir en esa decisión.
Cole alcanza un hito que ningún número 1 del draft ha logrado nunca
No fue hasta que los Yankees sentenciaron el partido cuando la noche de Cole pasó a ocupar un lugar más destacado en la historia de la MLB. Esa victoria fue la número 162 de su carrera, lo que le permitió superar a Mike Moore como el lanzador con más victorias de todos los seleccionados en el número 1 del draft de la MLB. Pittsburgh eligió a Cole como primera elección en 2011. Moore, elegido en primer lugar por Seattle en 1981, terminó con 161 victorias. David Price ocupa el tercer puesto entre los lanzadores elegidos en el número 1 del draft, con 157.
Este hito vino acompañado de una advertencia de octubre que aún pesaba. Corbin Carroll conectó un jonrón de dos carreras en la segunda entrada con una bola rápida de cuatro costuras que no llegó donde debía. Fue el único daño que Arizona le hizo a Cole, pero ese lanzamiento fue importante por lo que había pasado justo antes del viernes.
Cole había encajado siete jonrones en sus dos últimas salidas, la mayor cantidad que había permitido nunca en un periodo de dos salidas. Cuatro de esos siete fueron con bolas rápidas de cuatro costuras. Si sumas el jonrón de Carroll, cinco de los ocho jonrones que el as de los Yankees ha encajado en sus últimas tres salidas han sido con la bola rápida de cuatro costuras.
El problema del lanzamiento de cuatro costuras se ha reducido, pero no ha desaparecido
Cole ha encajado 10 jonrones en sus últimas seis salidas, en las que ha cedido 18 carreras en 34 2/3 entradas. Su balance es de 9-9, con una efectividad de 3,63, un WHIP de 1,10 y 123 ponches frente a 22 bases por bolas en 121 1/3 entradas y 21 salidas como titular.
Antes de las malas salidas contra San Diego y los Mets, Cole tenía una efectividad de 3,29 en 18 aperturas. En las cuatro aperturas previas al viernes, los bateadores habían conseguido 16 de 48 contra su bola rápida de cuatro costuras, mientras que en sus primeras 16 aperturas habían conseguido 32 de 173 contra ella.
El as de los Yankees ha registrado una tasa de strikes fallidos del 11,6 % con su lanzamiento de cuatro costuras en las tres salidas que llevaba hasta el viernes, por debajo del 22,8 % que había logrado en sus primeras 17 salidas. Los Yankees necesitaban pruebas de que ese lanzamiento volviera a funcionar contra bateadores del nivel de la postemporada.
Boone mantiene a Cole en los planes de los Yankees para octubre
Aaron Boone ya había dejado claro que dos malas salidas no iban a dejar fuera a Cole de la rotación de los Yankees para la postemporada. Tras la derrota de los Yankees ante los Mets, Boone dejó claras sus expectativas.
«Espero que la próxima vez acierte», dijo Boone.
Lo del viernes no ha cambiado el plan general de Boone para octubre. Cuando le preguntaron si Cole debería contar con ser titular si los Yankees llegan a la Serie de Comodines, el entrenador volvió a respaldarlo.
«Sí, espero que Gerrit Cole sea el abridor», dijo Boone.
La cuestión más importante es qué versión de la bola rápida de Cole le acompañará. El analista de YES Network, David Cone, había señalado los lanzamientos secundarios, diciendo que los bateadores se habían acostumbrado a esperar la bola rápida.
«No respetan tus lanzamientos secundarios, están esperando tu bola rápida», dijo Cone.
Una salida más supone una prueba a la altura de octubre
Cole tiene prevista una salida más en la temporada regular, en casa contra los Rays la semana que viene. Esa salida puede dar a los Yankees una idea más clara antes de organizar su plantilla de lanzadores de cara a una posible serie de comodín al mejor de tres.
El viernes se dieron pasos importantes. El as de los Yankees atacó la zona de strike, no concedió ninguna base por bolas y mantuvo a raya a Arizona tras el golpe de Carroll en la segunda entrada. Además, los Yankees limitaron su carga de trabajo a 90 lanzamientos.
Pero la pregunta sobre el jonrón le siguió hasta salir del Chase Field. Cole hizo historia en la MLB y recuperó algo de confianza en la misma noche. La bola rápida de cuatro costuras aún tiene una última prueba en septiembre antes de que los Yankees decidan hasta qué punto pueden confiar en ella en octubre.
¿Qué te parece? Deja tu comentario más abajo.

item.content:encoded:
PHOENIX — While Friday wasn’t a positive day in terms of injury news for the Aaron Judge-less Yankees, Aaron Boone did say that the team can count on a reinforcement soon.
That would be Jazz Chisholm Jr., who is expected to return from a sprained right thumb on the team’s upcoming and final homestand of the regular season. Boone said that Friday was the second baseman’s fourth day of hitting in a row. He’s also been throwing the last few days.
“He’s getting very close,” Boone said.
Chisholm previously said that he hoped to come off the injured list when the Yankees returned home from Arizona. He hurt his thumb while sliding into second base on Sept. 8.
Chisholm is an impending free agent in the midst of a disappointing season, but he had rounded into form before getting. He hit .295 with an .832 OPS, three home runs, 10 RBI and 10 stolen bases over his last 29 games. He also had a .391 OPS and a 1.028 OPS over his last 15 games.
The hope is that Chisholm can pick up where he left off, especially with Judge returning to the IL with a right calf strain.
Chisholm is hitting .232 with a .715 OPS, 19 home runs, 55 RBI and 40 steals overall.
GRISHAM ‘COULD BE IN PLAY’
Boone also said that Trent Grisham is pretty far into his running progression and “could be in play at the end of the season.” The center fielder suffered his second right hamstring strain of the season earlier this month.
Prior to that, Grisham hit .211 with a .703 OPS and 18 home runs. He’s also been one of the slowest and worst defensive center fielders in baseball the last two years.
With Grisham not producing on either side of the ball and Spencer Jones more than holding his own, the former was not guaranteed to start in the playoffs prior to Judge’s injury. Now, however, Grisham could play center while Jones handles right. The Yankees can also use Jones in center and Heliot Ramos is right against lefties.
WEATHERS WON’T RETURN BEFORE PLAYOFFS
While the Yankees had hoped otherwise, Aaron Boone said Ryan Weathers is “unlikely” to return before the end of the regular season. The left-handed starter, working his way back from a flexor strain as a reliever, is expected to throw his second bullpen session at Chase Field on Saturday.
Asked if the Yankees would be comfortable having Weathers’ first game off the IL come in the postseason, neither Boone nor pitching coach Matt Blake ruled the idea out.
“I don’t know if ‘comfortable’ is [the right word],” Blake said, “but it might be the course of action where he’s the best option even though he hasn’t pitched in the last three or four weeks.”

item.content:encoded:
MLB Trade Rumors | Darragh McDonald: Well, it was nice while it lasted. The Yankees announced yesterday evening that they will be placing right fielder Aaron Judge on the ten-day injured list with a calf strain today; Max Schuemann is expected to be the corresponding move. Since it will be backdated to the 16th, Judge will be eligible to come off the IL for the final day of the season; however, given the nature of calf strains, it is entirely possible that we have seen the last of No. 99 for 2026.
New York Daily News | Gary Phillips: Arguably the biggest surprise of the 2026 season — beyond the fact that the Yankees somehow managed to keep their heads above water despite Aaron Judge missing three months, of course — has been the breakout of outfielder Spencer Jones. The former top prospect has managed to position himself as “a key cog in the Yankees’ lineup,” taking advantage of opportunities offered by injuries to Judge, Trent Grisham, Cody Bellinger, and Giancarlo Stanton. In particular, his performance against southpaws, which had long been a weakness throughout his minor league career, has been a pleasant surprise. That being said, it hasn’t been all sunshine and roses: Jones has yet to flash the leather in the way many have expected him to. Even so, however, it seems likely that Jones will be a critical part of the team’s postseason run, whether as the starting center fielder or a key reserve.
MLB.com | Mike Lupica: For all the attention that the Yankees’ veteran stars — Judge, Gerrit Cole, Max Fried, and Giancarlo Stanton — receive, the 2026 season has been a veritable youth movement. Key to that has been the development, of course, of first baseman/designated hitter Ben Rice and AL Cy Young frontrunner Cam Schlittler. The two youngsters from Massachusetts, never highly rated as prospects, have turned themselves into veritable forces at the plate and on the mound, and without their contributions, the injury-riddled 2026 Yankees would almost certainly be spending the final few days of the season playing out the string, not attempting to make a last-ditch run at the AL East while lining up the rotation for a matchup with the Red Sox in the Wild Card round.
MLB Trade Rumors | Darragh McDonald: Yesterday afternoon, the Yankees announced that Oswaldo Cabrera, the popular utilityman who has been with the organization since 2015, had been claimed off waivers by the Cincinnati Reds. He had been designated for assignment earlier in the week, in order to make room on the 40-man roster for Clarke Schmidt.
Playbill | Logan Culwell-Block: Earlier this summer, former Mets infielder José Iglesias made the jump from the ballfield to the stage, joining the Broadway production of Buena Vista Social Club. Now, a Yankee great will be joining him: yesterday, Bernie Williams announced that he will be joining the show’s pit band for a limited run, from October 22nd through November 29th.

item.content:encoded:
PHOENIX — Aaron Judge is on the injured list again, but the Yankees could get two key pieces back off of it by next week.
Jazz Chisholm Jr. should be activated on the upcoming homestand that begins Tuesday, Aaron Boone said Friday, after the second baseman landed on the IL last week with a right thumb sprain.




Access the Yankees beat like never before


Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees.
Try it free
Friday marked his fourth day of hitting in a row after being shut down from baseball activities for about a week, while he has also been throwing the last couple of days.
“He’s getting very close,” Boone said before the Yankees’ 9-2 win over the Diamondbacks at Chase Field.
Trent Grisham, meanwhile, is “pretty far into his running progression” from a right hamstring strain and “doing well,” Boone said, putting him in position to be in play at the end of the regular season.
Before Judge’s calf strain, it was questionable whether there would be a lane for Grisham to get playing time if and when he returned.
But now it is possible he could return to center field at least against righties, bumping Spencer Jones to right field.
As for Ryan Weathers, the other Yankee trying to make it back in time for the playoffs (from a left forearm flexor strain), Boone acknowledged the lefty is “unlikely to get into a game before the end of the season.”
Weathers is set to throw a second bullpen session on Saturday, after which he could advance to facing hitters in live batting practice.
Whether that will give him enough time to show he should be part of the bullpen for the first round of the playoffs remains to be seen.
“We’ll see what our needs are and how he looks and if we feel like he’s ready to come in and be a contributor,” Boone said.
Anthony Volpe, who was back at second base, hit .348 with a .965 OPS and four steals in his first seven games since being called back up from Triple-A as an injury replacement for Chisholm.
He was 0-for-4 in Friday night’s win.

item.title: [Pinstripe Alley] Yankees ride five-run first to series-opening romp of Diamondbacks
item.dc:creator: Peter Brody
item.description: The two starting pitchers entered this game trending in opposite directions. Gerrit Cole had just allowed the most home runs (seven) in a two-start span in his career, while Eduardo Rodriguez is in the midst of a career year with a 2.62 ERA. One of those trends remained — Cole giving up another home run on a fastball — but fortunately the other trend was momentarily halted, the Yankees scoring five in the first off E-Rod to give themselves enough of a cushion to weather Cole’s continued home run
item.content:encoded:
The two starting pitchers entered this game trending in opposite directions. Gerrit Cole had just allowed the most home runs (seven) in a two-start span in his career, while Eduardo Rodriguez is in the midst of a career year with a 2.62 ERA. One of those trends remained — Cole giving up another home run on a fastball — but fortunately the other trend was momentarily halted, the Yankees scoring five in the first off E-Rod to give themselves enough of a cushion to weather Cole’s continued home run woes.
Cole settled down after the Carroll dinger to give the Yankees six innings, by which time the offense all but put this game out of reach. They kept the pressure on, scoring a further four runs including solo home runs by Ben Rice and George Lombard Jr., to cruise to a series-opening victory in the desert, 9-2.
Rodriguez came into this game with an ERA above six in the first inning and an ERA right around two for the subsequent innings combined. That made it imperative that the Yankees find a way to do damage before the home team had a chance to come to bat, especially with the rate Cole is giving up the long ball. They did just that with a clear disciplined approach not to expand the zone against E-Rod’s curveball.
Paul Goldschmidt drew a leadoff walk, Cody Bellinger followed with a single, and Heliot Ramos also walked to load the bases with no outs. Rice drew the Yankees’ third walk in the first four batters to plate Goldschmidt and open the scoring, Goldy, Ramos, and Rice all working full counts before taking the free pass. Amed Rosario then fought off a cutter that handcuffed him up and in, muscling it to the opposite field perfectly between center and left fielder to plate Bellinger as the runners went station to station. A wild pitch allowed Ramos to score and Rice and Rosario to move up to second and third. This set up a two-run ground ball single from Lombard that just got by Geraldo Perdomo’s diving attempt to atone for his defensive misplay in the 13th that allowed the Twins to walk off the Yankees on Wednesday.
Rodriguez struck out Volpe to end the inning giving him three strikeouts in the frame, but the damage was done. The 45 pitches he threw were the most he’s thrown in the first inning in his career. 33 of those pitches fell out of the zone, but only eight induced a chase.
It’s a good thing they hung such a crooked number, because Cole immediately gave two of those runs back. He gave up a leadoff single to Perdomo before yanking an 0-1 four-seamer right into Corbin Carroll’s nitro zone, the three-time All-Star obliterating it to right for a two-run bomb to reduce the Yankees’ lead, 5-2. Rice made sure to immediately tilt the momentum back in his team’s favor. After falling behind 0-2, he stayed back on an elevated heater from E-Rod riding it out the other way and over the fence in left-center for a leadoff bomb, his 39th of the year, to give Cole some more of his cushion back, 6-2.
Cole settled down to work a scoreless third and fourth, helped in part by a sharp uptick in slider usage at the expense of some four-seamers as well as an impressive sliding catch in left-center by Spencer Jones in the third. He finally began dialing the fastball command to the corners in the fifth, striking out Tim Tawa and Lars Nootbaar on four-seamers to end the frame after Jesús Sánchez singled with one out. This allowed Lombard to restore the Yankees’ five run lead in the sixth, the rookie punishing a hanging curveball from E-Rod by lining the solo shot down the line it left and into the bullpen for his fourth of the year and third RBI on the night.
The four-seamer was the prime culprit for Cole in his previous two starts with a 68.2-percent hard-hit rate and just six whiffs, and that remained the case tonight. However, I believe it is Cole’s rustiness with his secondaries that is leading his four-seamer to get barreled. The fastball still has plenty of velocity — at 97 mph it’s a full tick above last season. I will grant that he has missed location in the zone on numerous occasions which hasn’t done him any favors.
However, after his last start, Cole identified a lack of chase and whiff against his secondaries as the reason his fastball is getting crushed. Hitters being able to lay off those chase pitches forces Cole to overuse the fastball in counts that favor the softer stuff, which in essence gives them the opportunity to hunt the heater when they should be defending against the breaker. When you can hunt a fastball in any count, chances are you are going to do damage when Cole misses his spot in the zone, the high velocity not much of a weapon when hitters’ bats are preemptively sped up.
Indeed, once he started commanding his slider and knuckle curve to the shadow of the zone in the middle innings, the hard contact against the fastball dried up. Having pitched a strong fifth and sixth and with his pitch count at 90, Boone saw no reason to overextend Cole and ended his night after six with his best innings freshest in mind. He finished night having pitched six innings, allowing two runs on four hits with no walks and six strikeouts.
Despite possessing one of the stingiest bullpens in baseball, the Diamondbacks decided that a five-run deficit in the seventh was too steep to justify using their high leverage arms. So, Zac Gallen made his first career relief appearance, the former All-Star in the midst of am injury-plagued, below-replacement-level campaign. He allowed a leadoff single to Goldschmidt and walked Ramos and Rice — again, both in full counts — to load the bases with one out. Aaron Boone sent out Ryan McMahon to pinch-hit for Rosario, and he hit a sharp grounder to first that Pavin Smith gloved but airmailed the underhand toss to Gallen covering first as all the runners were safe and a run scored on the error. Spencer Jones then appeared to ground into the inning-ending double play, but his hustle out of the box and down the line just beat the throw to pick up an RBI and make it 9-2.
Ryan Yarbrough pitched 1.1 innings in relief of Cole and worked himself into and out of trouble in the seventh. Arizona put runners on second and third as Nolan Arenado singled and Carroll doubled with one out. However, Yarbrough struck out Jose Fernandez and Tawa to strand the pair in scoring position. Rice smoked his fourth triple of the year in the ninth but was stranded at third by a McMahon strikeout. Michael Fulmer and Luis Gil recorded the final five outs of the game without allowing a baserunner to seal the win, 9-2. With the Rays having lost to the Red Sox earlier in the evening, the Yankees’ deficit is back to four games in the division, making that looming four-game set against Tampa in the Bronx even more high stakes.
Cam Schlittler looks to cement his AL Cy Young case tomorrow after Dylan Cease suffered his shortest start of the season on Friday. The Yankees ace will face off against Brandon Pfaadt with a slightly more reasonable game start time. First pitch is scheduled for 8:10 pm ET with the broadcast remaining on YES.
Yankees rout the D-Backs, 9-2, who's your Player of the Game?
Gerrit Cole pitched 6 innings of 2-run ball. George Lombard Jr. hit a two-run single and a solo homer. Ben Rice raked with a solo homer, triple, and two walks.

After falling 5-4 to the Minnesota Twins on Wednesday, the club posted its lineup for the first game against the Diamondbacks, and the most notable tweak involved Spencer Jones, via FantasyPros. Jones had occupied the fifth spot in the order against Minnesota and finished without a hit while st
item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees open a series in Arizona on Friday night looking to rebound from a one-run loss and find more consistent production from a young outfielder who has shown both power and growing pains.
After falling 5-4 to the Minnesota Twins on Wednesday, the club posted its lineup for the first game against the Diamondbacks, and the most notable tweak involved Spencer Jones, via FantasyPros.
Jones had occupied the fifth spot in the order against Minnesota and finished without a hit while striking out five times. That performance prompted manager Aaron Boone to slide the 25-year-old down one place, into the sixth hole, for Friday’s contest.
The rest of the order features Paul Goldschmidt at first, Cody Bellinger in left, Heliot Ramos in right, Ben Rice as the designated hitter, Amed Rosario at third, George Lombard at short, Austin Wells behind the plate and Anthony Volpe at second. Jones will patrol center field.
The adjustment is modest on paper, yet it reflects the reality of a rookie season that has mixed encouraging numbers with stretches of swing-and-miss. Jones is hitting .252 with 59 hits, 10 home runs, 37 RBIs, 32 runs and nine stolen bases across 79 games.
Those totals represent real production for a player who made his major-league debut earlier this year after being selected in the first round of the 2022 draft out of Vanderbilt.
At 6-foot-7, 240 pounds, he possesses the kind of raw power that can change a game in a single swing, something he demonstrated with a three-run homer against the Twins just a few days earlier.
Still, five strikeouts in one night is the kind of night that forces a lineup shuffle. Boone has moved Jones around the order several times this season as the Yankees try to maximize his strengths while limiting damage against certain pitching looks.
The Diamondbacks series offers another chance to see whether a slightly lower spot in the batting order helps him settle in and put the ball in play more often.
New York arrives in Phoenix needing wins as the calendar moves deeper into September. A tight loss in Minnesota left little margin, and every at-bat from a developing bat like Jones carries extra weight.
The organization drafted him for his combination of size, athleticism and power; the challenge now is translating that package into more consistent contact at the highest level.
Friday’s lineup is a small tactical step in that process rather than a dramatic demotion.
Whether Jones responds with extra-base hits or continues to chase pitches remains to be seen. What is clear is that the Yankees still view him as part of their present and future outfield mix.
A drop from fifth to sixth is not a verdict on his season. It is simply the latest attempt to put a young player in a position where his next good swing can matter.

A fun weekend in prospect at Chase – at least, outside the lines, where the team will be celebrating the 25th anniversary of their World Series win against these same Yankees. The main party is taking place tomorrow night, but there are some things to note for tonight. Most relevantly to me who is recapping: Greg Schulte, the voice of the D-backs from their first Opening Day in 1998, through the end of the 2023 World Series, is making a return to the booth tonight. I've no idea how the sync between that and the TV broadcast will work out, but I think I am prepared to handle a little bit of lag for the evening.
With it being Friday night, and since I'm being robbed of most of my usual Friday night entertainment for recappage purposes – no eighties DJ on Twitch, no B-movie about killer hippopotami (they missed a trick by not calling the latter, Hippocalypse Now) – I will once again be tucking into my cider selection. Worked out well enough last Friday night, if my (slightly blurry) recollections are anything to go by. I think I have one untried flavor from the selection pack, plus a couple of "regular" brands in the fridge. You have been warned. Tim should be back for the final series next weekend, both you and my liver will be pleased to hear. 🙂
Another narrative will be taking the first pitch of the game, with Paul Goldschmidt returning to Chase Field. I'm sure he'll still get a warm welcome, even though he is now 1,104 games (including the post-season) removed from the last time Goldy pulled on the Sedona Red. I was looked at the 2018 roster, and there aren't many people there who are still playing in the majors this season. Ketel Marte, obviously – he was the "baby" of the roster that year! – and Ildemaro Vargas, then still a rookie. A few starting pitchers, in Taijuan Walker, Robbie Ray and Patrick Corbin. That's about it, on a quick, non-structured glance. Let me know if I missed any!

item.content:encoded:
Yankees manager Aaron Boone delivered some injury updates ahead of Friday's series opener with the Diamondbacks in Arizona…
Jazz returning soon
Although the Yankees are losing Aaron Judge, likely, for the remainder of the regular season, they'll be activating Jazz Chisholm Jr. very soon.
Boone confirmed that the second baseman will return to the club during the team's final homestand, which starts Tuesday against the Tampa Bay Rays. The Yankees skipper said Chisholm is doing well and Friday was his fourth day in a row hitting. He's done a couple of days of throwing already and is "really close."
Chisholm was placed on the IL back on Sept. 10 with a sprained thumb after he jammed it sliding head-first into second base.
The Yankees infielder was on a tear before he was injured, slashing .375/.464/.500 with a home run over his last seven games. For the season, he's batting .232/.312/.403 with an OPS of .715 to go along with his 19 home runs, 40 stolen bases and 55 RBI.
The return of Chisholm would raise some questions regarding the team's roster. While Chisholm could take over for Max Schuemann, who is being called up to take Judge's spot, Anthony Volpe has been playing second base almost regularly in Chisholm's stead. How Boone juggles the playing time for both players will be worth monitoring.
Bad Weathers
On the other side of the return spectrum, LHP Ryan Weathers is "unlikely" to pitch before the end of the regular season, Boone revealed.
Weathers was placed on the IL in late August due to a left forearm flexor strain, and although the southpaw has made strides, there's not enough time on the regular season calendar to get him on the mound before the postseason starts. Boone did say that Weathers will have another side session on Saturday, and that could determine whether the team will use him in the playoffs.
"We'll see what our needs are and how he looks, and if we feel like he's ready to come in and be a contributor," Boone said.
In 25 starts this season, Weathers has pitched to a 3.60 ERA and a 1.22 WHIP. His last seven starts have been tremendous, though, pitching to a 2.27 ERA and a 1.18 WHIP.
Grisham rising
And finally, Trent Grisham is nearing a return as well.
Boone said the veteran outfielder is "pretty far" into his running progression and is doing well. He could be in play to be activated before the end of the season.
Grisham was placed on the IL on Sept. 5 with a right hamstring strain, the same injury he suffered back in June this season. If Grisham is able to return on the upcoming homestand, Boone will, again, have to juggle the roster as Spencer Jones and Heliot Ramos have played regularly in his absence. Though Judge's injury gives Grisham a runway to start, especially against right-handers.
In 121 games this season, Grisham is slashing .211/.308/.395 with an OPS of .703.

item.title: [New York Post] Aaron Judge lands on IL with calf strain in Yankees nightmare — as huge playoff question emerges
item.dc:creator: Greg Joyce
item.description: Aaron Judge is going on the 10-day injured list with a right calf strain, the Yankees announced Friday, just seven games after he returned from a three-month stay on the IL with a right rib stress fracture. Access the Yankees beat like never before Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees. With only nine games left in the regular season after Friday, Judge’s injury threatens to be a serious blow to t
item.content:encoded:
Aaron Judge is going on the 10-day injured list with a right calf strain, the Yankees announced Friday, just seven games after he returned from a three-month stay on the IL with a right rib stress fracture.
Access the Yankees beat like never before
Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees.
With only nine games left in the regular season after Friday, Judge’s injury threatens to be a serious blow to the Yankees’ October hopes and dreams.
The earliest Judge can be activated off the IL — he will officially be placed on it Saturday, but retroactive to Thursday — is in time for Game 162, though there is doubt over whether he will even be ready in time for the start of the playoffs.
“I don’t know,” Aaron Boone said Friday at Chase Field.
Boone would not divulge a timeline for Judge, nor the grade of his strain. But after he received treatment on his calf during Thursday’s off day, it became clear there was not enough improvement, at which point they decided to send him for tests that revealed the strain.
The AL wild-card series, which the Yankees are all but assured to play in with their chances of catching the Rays for the division slim, begins on Sept. 29. Once again, Judge will be racing the clock to try to get back in time, creating major concerns for the Yankees as they head down the stretch without their best player.
“There’s no replacing a player as great as Aaron Judge, but we have high expectations that don’t change now,” Boone said. “We have a lot of confidence in the people we run out there every day and how we’re going to match up day in and day out, and the goal doesn’t change.”
When Judge spent most of the summer months on the IL, the Yankees’ offense largely cratered without him, though they had started to break out of their malaise shortly before he returned on Sept. 8.
Judge’s injury will create further scrutiny as to whether he should have gone on a rehab assignment instead of coming straight back into games. The captain was adamant about not wanting to waste time playing in minor league games, and the Yankees – who could not force Judge to go on a rehab assignment – tried to ease him back in carefully. They played him for six innings his first game back – much to his chagrin – then eight innings, then an off day. Judge then played four straight games through Monday’s playoff clincher before the Yankees sat him again on Tuesday, after which they were hopeful he would essentially be a full go.
But then came the nightmare, when Judge felt some calf tightness while playing the field in the bottom of the first inning and then by the top of the sixth, was pinch hit for by Heliot Ramos.
Before the injury, Judge was still trying to lock in his timing at the plate after a long layoff, batting 4-for-23 (.174) with a .513 OPS and one home run. These final three series were supposed to be about getting him in a good spot for the postseason, but now he will spend them getting treatment and rehabbing in hopes of playing again.
Fellow Yankees slugger Giancarlo Stanton suffered a calf strain in late April and has not played another game since, though he was initially on the verge of a return in June before suffering two more calf strains since.
Judge, after leaving Wednesday’s game against the Twins early, likened the issue to something he would deal with in spring training while building up his workload, except it is now September.
In the meantime, the Yankees started Ramos in right field on Friday against Diamondbacks lefty Eduardo Rodríguez, and he will likely get the majority of the time there down the stretch.
Even before Judge’s injury, the Yankees were already dealing with a few players trying to make a comeback in time for the playoffs, including Jazz Chisholm Jr. (right thumb sprain), Trent Grisham (right hamstring strain) and Ryan Weathers (left forearm flexor strain). Grisham, who could be ready by next week, now has a potential lane to come back in center field, bumping Spencer Jones to right. Chisholm is also expected to be activated when the Yankees return home.
Max Schuemann will join the Yankees on Saturday to take Judge’s roster spot.
“We’re gonna have to find a way,” Cody Bellinger said. “I think the talent in this locker room speaks for itself, and I’m fully confident that we have enough talent in here that we can go out and win and beat anybody.”

So, Volpe's future in New York is very much up in the air. New York will begin a three-game road series against the Arizona Diamondbacks on Friday. New York Yankees Surprise Anthony Volpe Decision Although Volpe has been playing better, he isn't guaranteed a spot on the Yankees playoff roster. After New York clinched a pl
item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees could make a surprising move on Anthony Volpe.
Volpe has had success since being recalled, but George Lombard Jr. has taken over as the starting shortstop. So, Volpe's future in New York is very much up in the air.
New York will begin a three-game road series against the Arizona Diamondbacks on Friday.
New York Yankees Surprise Anthony Volpe Decision
Although Volpe has been playing better, he isn't guaranteed a spot on the Yankees playoff roster.
After New York clinched a playoff spot, Yankees analysts Bryan Hoch and Patrick Donnelly of MLB.com revealed the likely playoff roster, and they didn't have Volpe on it.
What could the postseason roster look like?
C: Austin Wells, Ali Sánchez
1B: Luis García Jr., Paul Goldschmidt
2B: Jazz Chisholm Jr.
3B: Ryan McMahon, Amed Rosario
SS: George Lombard Jr., José Caballero
OF: Cody Bellinger, Spencer Jones, Aaron Judge, Heliot Ramos
DH: Ben Rice
SP: Cam Schlittler, Max Fried, Gerrit Cole
RP: David Bednar, Brent Headrick, Paul Blackburn, Tim Hill, Ryan Yarbrough, Clarke Schmidt, Michael Fulmer, Ryan Weathers, Will Warren
The Yankees leaving Volpe off the playoff roster would be a disappointing outcome for the shortstop. It also could signal the end of his tenure in New York as Lombard is the shortstop of the future.
Volpe is hitting .253 with 2 home runs and 26 RBIs this season with the Yankees.
New York Right Now
The Yankees have clinched a playoff spot as New York will be hosting a Wild Card series again.
"Every year you go through a lot, it seems like. But we've been through a lot this year with injuries, with adversity," Yankees manager Aaron Boone said. "But credit to them for coming together. Through all the ups and downs, they've been a together group. I feel like they've developed a lot of grit over the season."
However, despite clinching a playoff spot, the Yankees made it clear the job isn't finished. New York likely won't win the AL East again, which is frustrating, but the Yankees have confidence they can go on a deep playoff run.
The Yankees are 88-64 and 5 games back of the Tampa Bay Rays for the top spot in the AL East.
